newsitem.title: UK: EMU still well on course -- Reuters survey.
newsitem.headline: EMU still well on course -- Reuters survey.

text.p: The odds of European currency union proceeding on time are still very favourable, despite a slight narrowing in January, a Reuters survey of predictions by EMU analysts showed on Wednesday. Thirty bank economists, academics and political analysts who took part gave on average an 83 percent chance of a single currency being launched by the target date of January 1, 1999, a three-point drop from 86 percent in December.
Analysts in the November poll gave an average 82 percent likelihood of EMU starting on its scheduled date, while in the first survey in October, the odds were put at 80 percent.

The analysts said there was little significance in the slight slip from December, which was the most bullish month for EMU prospects as reflected by the monthly barometer since Reuters started it in October 1996.
The December update came shortly after EU leaders gave EMU's prospects a healthy boost by agreeing at a summit in Dublin to a stability pact which set the rules for currency union.
"There is little to have happened in the past month which alters the view on EMU," said Carls Hamilton, chief economist at Svenska Handelsbanken in Stockholm.
All 30 analysts agreed that EMU would be launched with a core group of six countries -- Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
The odds for Finland and Ireland joining were also highly favourable, with 26 of the 30 giving Ireland the nod and 23 saying the Finnish markka would take part from the outset.

Contributor expectations for Spain and Portugal joining the core group in 1999 were little changed at averages of 30 percent and 27 percent respectively, but prospects dimmed for Italy, according to the survey.
The average expectation for Italy joining EMU from the start fell to 16 percent in January from 22 percent.

"Spain and Portugal are looking a lot more likely. There has been a change of perception -- before Spain and Portugal were considered together with Italy. Now they are considered separately," said Steve Englander, of Smith Barney in Paris.
The analysts said both Spain and Portugal were coming close to the economic targets for entry to EMU which the newly-wrought stability pact is designed to regulate.

Under the terms of the pact, countries which run a budget deficit of more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) will face sanctions and fines, but economists fear that there are too many loopholes.
"A special deal is likely from some "near-ins" such as Italy, and possibly Portugal and Spain, in lieu of full membership," said Daniel Gros, of Belgium's Centre for Economic Policy Studies.

"If the budgetary criteria are construed generously enough to admit Belgium, it would be hard to refuse Spain, Portugal and Italy," said John Arrowsmith, at Britain's National Institute for Economic and Social Research (NIESR).
Belgium last week denied accusations from two academics that the Treasury had massaged debt figures to improve the chances of qualifying for a single European currency.
